The explanation of why a conclusion was reached (e.g. relevant legislation or tribunal decision); not required to be stated and not appealable.

caveats: Guidance describes typical/expected bookkeeping practice for HMRC enquiry officers assessing record quality; it is not a legal requirement specifying what records taxpayers must keep.
Notes that even computerised or double-entry systems do not guarantee accuracy of figures; the integrity of records depends on underlying data, not the system used.

definitions.meaning: A record of payments and receipts from and into the bank account; receipts are debited and credited to the appropriate ledger, payments are credited and debited to the appropriate ledger.
Details withdrawals of cash and payments for small expenditure, with cash expenditure debited to appropriate nominal ledger accounts.
Prime records written up from sales or purchases invoices, usually in chronological order, cross-referenced to invoices and the relevant ledger account.
A summary of the totals of a ledger for a given period, used to prove the arithmetical accuracy of that ledger; does not form part of the double-entry.

Books used day to day to record the bulk of business transactions, not part of the double-entry system itself: sales day book, purchases day book, petty cash book, sales/purchases returns books, wages book.
The ledgers comprising cash book (including bank account), sales ledger, purchase ledger, and nominal ledger, where every transaction is recorded as both a debit and a credit.
A process to prove the accuracy of the bank balance in the accounts, ensuring all entries in the cash book and bank statements have been accounted for.

note.summary: This chunk from HMRC's Enquiry Manual describes how small businesses typically keep records (proprietary record books, simple ledgers, computerised systems) and how accountants construct accounts from incomplete records using cash and bank control accounts. It explains single-entry versus double-entry bookkeeping, the structure of prime records (sales/purchases day books, petty cash, wages book) versus double-entry ledgers (cash book, sales/purchase ledgers, nominal ledger), and how transactions flow through these systems including reconciliations. It is guidance for HMRC officers conducting enquiries into how a taxpayer's accounts were prepared, not a statement of statutory obligations.

2b387d5ec00a7b6b.heading: Enquiry Manual (EM) > What is a matter

caveats: PCN can only be used to complete enquiry into a matter where the matter is discrete/self-contained and can be made final without affecting other matters under enquiry.
Description of a matter in a PCN should not include conclusions or potential amendments to tax calculations.
A customer may appeal against any conclusion or amendment stated in a closure notice, but not against the stated 'reasons'.

If conclusions are stated too narrowly and rejected by courts, HMRC may be barred from introducing other technical arguments; if stated too widely, taxpayer may be allowed to introduce broader arguments - officers must balance precision.
In complex avoidance cases, the 'matter' may be the overall arrangement rather than each individual amount deducted.
Alternative conclusions in complex cases require contacting TALA for advice if taxpayer agreement to a joint referral cannot be obtained.
cross_references: Fidex Limited v HMRC [2016] EWCA Civ 385

definitions.meaning: Any part of the return that can become final by being amended but without affecting other parts of the tax return or being affected by other parts of the tax return; could be a single entry, several entries considered together, or a supplementary page.
definitions.ref: EM Enquiry Manual - What is a matter

definitions.meaning: Notice by which an officer informs the taxpayer that they have completed enquiries into the return.
Notice by which an officer informs the taxpayer that they have completed their enquiry into a matter.
The changes made to entries in the partnership tax return or partnership statement to give effect to conclusions stated in a closure notice; it is the closure notice itself that amends the return.
The decision reached about what needs to be amended in the return, explaining the officer's view on how the return is incorrect and, where appropriate, the correct treatment.
Explanation of why a conclusion has been reached, e.g. relevant legislation or tribunal decision relied on; not required to be stated but considered good practice.
The questions that the tribunal can consider during an appeal hearing, defined by the conclusions stated in the closure notice and the amendments required to give effect to those conclusions.
definitions.ref: EM7563, citing Fidex Limited v HMRC [2016] EWCA Civ 385 [45]

It covers the PCN101 approval process, and then details final closure notices (FCNs), partnership return amendments, the concept of 'conclusions' and 'reasons' in closure notices, and the scope of appeals as defined by closure notice conclusions (citing Fidex Limited v HMRC). It also addresses consequential amendments to partners' returns following partnership closure notices under TMA70/s.28B(4) and TMA70/s.30B(2).

note.summary: This HMRC Enquiry Manual page lists the compliance check factsheets (CC/FS series) and other notices HMRC officers must issue to taxpayers, specifying the trigger event and timing for each. By concession, the tax adjustment in the averaging example is based on £10,000 rather than the strictly correct £12,000, to avoid reopening originally returned figures.

Family wages late deduction claims are usually difficult to sustain absent supporting evidence; example figures (£16,000/£30,000 etc.) relate to tax years 2003/4 and 2004/5 and are illustrative only, not current rates.
SA interest rules apply automatically for assessments raised after 5 April 1998, with exceptions for 1996/97 partnership assessments.

Discovery assessments are used to recover tax loss when enquiry time limits have passed or no return was submitted, subject to conditions, and the Supreme Court in HMRC v Tooth confirmed discoveries cannot become 'stale' and there is no collective knowledge principle within HMRC. If the deceased partner's return has not been filed when a s.30B discovery amendment is made, failure to act (e.g. consider a determination) before the time limit may prevent HMRC giving effect to the s.30B(2) amendment.

Early finality on a deceased partner's return is only possible if the partnership has ceased, and confirming no enquiry into the partner's return effectively gives finality to the partnership return as well, so officers should weigh this carefully.

The EM8001 and EM8004 sections concern company (corporation tax) enquiries, not Self Assessment, and are included for context/manual navigation only; CTSA/company return rules differ by accounting period regime (CTA, CTPF, CTSA).

note.summary: This chunk covers HMRC's Enquiry Manual guidance on deceased partners in a partnership: enquiries into the partnership return continue after a partner's death, with consequential amendments to the deceased partner's return made under s.28B(4) (no time bar) or, following a discovery amendment, under s.30B(2) (time-barred four years after the year of assessment of death, extendable to six years before death for careless/deliberate behaviour). It distinguishes the deceased partner's pre-death SA return from any post-death trust and estate return made by the personal representative, to which s.28B(4)/s.30B(2) amendments cannot apply (only s.9A enquiry and s.28A closure notice). It also covers early finality requests on a partner's death, and separately introduces the manual's company enquiry chapters (EM8001, EM8004) which are not part of Self Assessment but explain CTSA scope and the company/participator distinction.
